papers.title: The effect of policy cancellation on the risk of an insurance portfolio
papers.abstract: For an insurance portfolio modelled by a large number of i.i.d. losses, the average loss converges to its expected value by the law of large numbers, reflecting the diversification effect of pooling risks. Policy cancellations reduce the portfolio size and thereby weaken this effect. We quantify the resulting increase in risk by applying risk measures to the average loss before and after the cancellation of policies. For a portfolio of size $n$, we show that the impact of cancelling a single contract is of order $n^{-3/2}$, while the cancellation of a fixed proportion of contracts has an effect of order $n^{-1/2}$. We further extend the proportional cancellation regime to heterogeneous portfolios with different cancellation rates and risk characteristics across segments. These asymptotic results provide a quantitative basis for assessing surrender fees and cancellation costs from the insurer's perspective. We complement the theoretical analysis with numerical results for representative life insurance products, illustrating the magnitude of cancellation costs and the effect of portfolio aggregation. The two regimes require different techniques. For the cancellation of a fixed proportion of contracts, we employ central limit theorems in Wasserstein distance. For the cancellation of a single contract, we combine Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality with higher-order distributional approximations based on the Edgeworth and Cornish-Fisher expansions.

papers.title: Dynamic Scenario-Based Portfolio Optimization for Multi-Asset ETFs
papers.abstract: Portfolio outcomes may depend as much on trading restrictions as on how returns are modeled. We compared historical moving-window returns with conditional scenarios from ARMA--GARCH models and a Student-$t$ copula for 30 U.S.-listed exchange-traded funds. Matched mean--variance and conditional value-at-risk portfolios were evaluated under long-only and limited long--short bounds over 946 sessions. Historical portfolios had higher observed reward--risk ratios in most comparisons, but no paired difference remained significant after multiple-testing adjustment. Conditional scenarios did not consistently reduce realized downside risk. We distinguished changes in target weights from trades required to rebalance holdings after market movements. Relaxing the target-adjustment limit changed exposures, turnover, and some returns more than varying scenario count or seed in the examined tests. These findings suggest that assessments of conditional return inputs should consider portfolio constraints and trading requirements.
